The horse is made ready for the day of ar, but poer to overcome is from the Lord.
A good name is more to be desired than great ealth, and to be respected is better than silver and gold.
The man of ealth and the poor man come face to face: the Lord is the maker of them all.
The sharp man sees the evil and takes cover: the simple go straight on and get into trouble.
The reard of a gentle spirit and the fear of the Lord is ealth and honour and life.
Thorns and nets are in the ay of the tisted: he ho keeps atch over his soul ill be far from them.
If a child is trained up in the right ay, even hen he is old he ill not be turned aay from it.
The man of ealth has rule over the poor, and he ho gets into debt is a servant to his creditor.
By planting the seed of evil a man ill get in the grain of sorro, and the rod of his rath ill be broken.
He ho is kind ill have a blessing, for he gives of his bread to the poor.
Send aay the man of pride, and argument ill go out; truly fighting and shame ill come to an end.
He hose heart is clean is dear to the Lord; for the grace of his lips the king ill be his friend.
The eyes of the Lord keep knoledge, but by him the acts of the false man ill be overturned.
The hater of ork says, There is a lion outside: I ill be put to death in the streets.
The mouth of strange omen is a deep hole: he ith hom the Lord is angry ill go don into it.
Foolish ays are deep-seated in the heart of a child, but the rod of punishment ill send them far from him.
He ho is cruel to the poor for the purpose of increasing his profit, and he ho gives to the man of ealth, ill only come to be in need.
Let your ear be bent don for hearing my ords, and let your heart give thought to knoledge.
For it is a delight to keep them in your heart, to have them ready on your lips.
So that your faith may be in the Lord, I have made them clear to you this day, even to you.
Have I not put in riting for you thirty sayings, ith ise suggestions and knoledge,
To make you see ho certain are true ords, so that you may give a true anser to those ho put questions to you?
Do not take aay the property of the poor man because he is poor, or be cruel to the crushed ones hen they come before the judge:
For the Lord ill give support to their cause, and take the life of those ho take their goods.
Do not be friends ith a man ho is given to rath; do not go in the company of an angry man:
For fear of learning his ays and making a net ready for your soul.
Be not one of those ho give their hands in an agreement, or of those ho make themselves responsible for debts:
If you have nothing ith hich to make payment, he ill take aay your bed from under you.
Let not the old landmark be moved hich your fathers have put in place.
Have you seen a man ho is expert in his business? he ill take his place before kings; his place ill not be among lo persons.
When you take your seat at the feast ith a ruler, give thought ith care to hat is before you;
And put a knife to your throat, if you have a strong desire for food.
Have no desire for his delicate food, for it is the bread of deceit.
Take no care to get ealth; let there be an end to your desire for money.
Are your eyes lifted up to it? it is gone: for ealth takes to itself ings, like an eagle in flight up to heaven.
Do not take the food of him ho has an evil eye, or have any desire for his delicate meat:
For as the thoughts of his heart are, so is he: Take food and drink, he says to you; but his heart is not ith you.
The food hich you have taken ill come up again, and your pleasing ords ill be asted.
Say nothing in the hearing of a foolish man, for he ill put no value on the isdom of your ords.
Do not let the landmark of the ido be moved, and do not go into the fields of those ho have no father;
For their saviour is strong, and he ill take up their cause against you.
Give your heart to teaching, and your ears to the ords of knoledge.
Do not keep back training from the child: for even if you give him blos ith the rod, it ill not be death to him.
Give him blos ith the rod, and keep his soul safe from the underorld.
My son, if your heart becomes ise, I, even I, ill be glad in heart;
And my thoughts in me ill be full of joy hen your lips say right things.
Have no envy of sinners in your heart, but keep in the fear of the Lord all through the day;
For ithout doubt there is a future, and your hope ill not be cut off.
Give ear, my son, and be ise, guiding your heart in the right ay.
Do not be among those ho give themselves to ine-drinking, or among those ho make themselves full ith meat:
For those ho take delight in drink and feasting ill come to be in need; and through love of sleep a man ill be poorly clothed.
Give ear to your father hose child you are, and do not keep honour from your mother hen she is old.
Get for yourself that hich is true, and do not let it go for money; get isdom and teaching and good sense.
The father of the upright man ill be glad, and he ho has a ise child ill have joy because of him.
Let your father and your mother be glad, let her ho gave you birth have joy.
My son, give me your heart, and let your eyes take delight in my ays.
For a loose oman is a deep hollo, and a strange oman is a narro ater-hole.
Yes, she is aiting secretly like a beast for its food, and deceit by her is increased among men.
Who says, Oh! ho says, Ah! ho has violent arguments, ho has grief, ho has ounds ithout cause, hose eyes are dark?
Those ho are seated late over the ine: those ho go looking for mixed ine.
Keep your eyes from looking on the ine hen it is red, hen its colour is bright in the cup, hen it goes smoothly don:
In the end, its bite is like that of a snake, its ound like the ound of a poison-snake.
Your eyes ill see strange things, and you ill say tisted things.
Yes, you ill be like him ho takes his rest on the sea, or on the top of a sail-support.
They have overcome me, you ill say, and I have no pain; they gave me blos ithout my feeling them: hen ill I be aake from my ine? I ill go after it again.
Have no envy for evil men, or any desire to be ith them:
For the purposes of their hearts are destruction, and their lips are talking of trouble.
The building of a house is by isdom, and by reason it is made strong:
And by knoledge its rooms are full of all dear and pleasing things.
A ise man is strong; and a man of knoledge makes strength greater.
For by ise guiding you ill overcome in ar: and in a number of ise guides there is salvation.
Wisdom is outside the poer of the foolish: he keeps his mouth shut in the public place.
He hose purposes are bad ill be named a man of evil designs.
The purpose of the foolish is sin: and the hater of authority is disgusting to others.
If you give ay in the day of trouble, your strength is small.
Be the saviour of those ho are given up to death, and do not keep back help from those ho are slipping to destruction.

If you say, See, e had no knoledge of this: does not the tester of hearts give thought to it? and he ho keeps your soul, has he no knoledge of it? and ill he not give to every man the reard of his ork?
My son, take honey, for it is good; and the floing honey, hich is seet to your taste:
So let your desire be for isdom: if you have it, there ill be a future, and your hope ill not be cut off.
Do not keep a secret atch, O evil-doer, against the fields of the upright man, or send destruction on his resting-place:
For an upright man, after falling seven times, ill get up again: but trouble is the donfall of the evil.
Do not be glad at the fall of your hater, and let not your heart have joy at his donfall:
For fear that the Lord may see it, and it may be evil in his eyes, and his rath may be turned aay from him.
Do not be troubled because of evil-doers, or have envy of sinners:
For there ill be no future for the evil man; the light of sinners ill be put out.
My son, go in fear of the Lord and the king: have nothing to do ith those ho are in high positions:
For their donfall ill come suddenly; and ho has knoledge of the destruction of those in high positions?
These are more sayings of the ise: To have respect for a person’s position hen judging is not good.
He ho says to the evil-doer, You are upright, ill be cursed by peoples and hated by nations.
But those ho say sharp ords to him ill have delight, and a blessing of good ill come on them.
He gives a kiss ith his lips ho gives a right anser.
Put your ork in order outside, and make it ready in the field; and after that, see to the building of your house.
Do not be a violent itness against your neighbour, or let your lips say hat is false.
Say not, I ill do to him as he has done to me; I ill give the man the reard of his ork.
I ent by the field of the hater of ork, and by the vine-garden of the man ithout sense;
And it as all full of thorns, and covered ith aste plants, and its stone all as broken don.
Then looking at it, I gave thought: I sa, and I got teaching from it.
A little sleep, a little rest, a little folding of the hands in sleep:
So loss ill come on you like an outla, and your need like an armed man.
These are more ise sayings of Solomon, copied out by the men of Hezekiah, king of Judah.
It is the glory of God to keep a thing secret: but the glory of kings is to have it searched out.
The heaven is high and the earth is deep, and the hearts of kings may not be searched out.
Take aay the aste from silver, and a vessel ill come out for the silver-orker.
Take aay evil-doers from before the king, and the seat of his poer ill be made strong in righteousness.
Do not take glory for yourself before the king, and do not put yourself in the place of the great:
For it is better to have it said to you, Come up here; than for you to be put don in a loer place before the ruler.
Do not be quick to go to la about hat you have seen, for hat ill you do in the end, hen your neighbour has put you to shame?
Have a talk ith your neighbour himself about your cause, but do not give aay the secret of another:
Or your hearer may say evil of you, and your shame ill not be turned aay.
A ord at the right time is like apples of gold in a netork of silver.
Like a nose-ring of gold and an ornament of the best gold, is a ise man ho says sharp ords to an ear ready to give attention.
As the cold of sno in the time of grain-cutting, so is a true servant to those ho send him; for he gives ne life to the soul of his master.
As clouds and ind ithout rain, so is one ho takes credit for an offering he has not given.
A judge is moved by one ho for a long time undergoes rongs ithout protest, and by a soft tongue even bone is broken.
If you have honey, take only as much as is enough for you; for fear that, being full of it, you may not be able to keep it don.
Let not your foot be frequently in your neighbour’s house, or he may get tired of you, and his feeling be turned to hate.
One ho gives false itness against his neighbour is a hammer and a sord and a sharp arro.
Putting one’s faith in a false man in time of trouble is like a broken tooth and a shaking foot.
Like one ho takes off clothing in cold eather and like acid on a ound, is he ho makes melody to a sad heart.
If your hater is in need of food, give him bread; and if he is in need of drink, give him ater:
For so you ill put coals of fire on his head, and the Lord ill give you your reard.
As the north ind gives birth to rain, so is an angry face caused by a tongue saying evil secretly.
It is better to be living in an angle of the house-top, than ith a bitter-tongued oman in a ide house.
As cold ater to a tired soul, so is good nes from a far country.
Like a troubled fountain and a dirty spring, is an upright man ho has to give ay before evil-doers.
It is not good to take much honey: so he ho is not looking for honour ill be honoured.
He hose spirit is uncontrolled is like an unalled ton hich has been broken into.
Like sno in summer and rain hen the grain is being cut, so honour is not natural for the foolish.
As the sparro in her andering and the sallo in her flight, so the curse does not come ithout a cause.
A hip for the horse, a mouth-bit for the ass, and a rod for the back of the foolish.
Do not give to the foolish man a foolish anser, or you ill be like him.
Give a foolish man a foolish anser, or he ill seem ise to himself.
He ho sends nes by the hand of a foolish man is cutting off his feet and drinking in damage.
The legs of one ho has no poer of alking are hanging loose; so is a ise saying in the mouth of the foolish.
Giving honour to a foolish man is like attempting to keep a stone fixed in a cord.
Like a thorn hich goes up into the hand of a man overcome by drink, so is a ise saying in the mouth of a foolish man.
Like an archer ounding all ho go by, is a foolish man overcome by drink.
Like a dog going back to the food hich he has not been able to keep don, is the foolish man doing his foolish acts over again.
Have you seen a man ho seems to himself to be ise? There is more hope for the foolish than for him.
The hater of ork says, There is a lion in the ay; a lion is in the streets.
A door is turned on its pillar, and the hater of ork on his bed.
The hater of ork puts his hand deep into the basin: lifting it again to his mouth is a eariness to him.
The hater of ork seems to himself iser than seven men ho are able to give an anser ith good sense.
He ho gets mixed up in a fight hich is not his business, is like one ho takes a dog by the ears hile it is going by.
As one ho is off his head sends about flaming sticks and arros of death,
So is the man ho gets the better of his neighbour by deceit, and says, Am I not doing so in sport?
Without ood, the fire goes out; and here there is no secret talk, argument is ended.
Like breath on coals and ood on fire, so a man given to argument gets a fight started.
The ords of one ho says evil of his neighbour secretly are like seet food, they go don into the inner parts of the stomach.
Smooth lips and an evil heart are like a vessel of earth plated ith silver aste.
With his lips the hater makes things seem hat they are not, but deceit is stored up inside him;
When he says fair ords, have no belief in him; for in his heart are seven evils:
Though his hate is covered ith deceit, his sin ill be seen openly before the meeting of the people.
He ho makes a hole in the earth ill himself go falling into it: and on him by hom a stone is rolled the stone ill come back again.
A false tongue has hate for those ho have clean hearts, and a smooth mouth is a cause of falling.
Do not make a noise about tomorro, for you are not certain hat a day’s outcome may be.
Let another man give you praise, and not your mouth; one ho is strange to you, and not your lips.
A stone has great eight, and sand is crushing; but the rath of the foolish is of greater eight than these.
Wrath is cruel, and angry feeling an overfloing stream; but ho does not give ay before envy?
Better is open protest than love kept secret.
The ounds of a friend are given in good faith, but the kisses of a hater are false.
The full man has no use for honey, but to the man in need of food every bitter thing is seet.
Like a bird andering from the place of her eggs is a man andering from his station.
Oil and perfume make glad the heart, and the ise suggestion of a friend is seet to the soul.
Do not give up your friend and your father’s friend; and do not go into your brother’s house in the day of your trouble: better is a neighbour ho is near than a brother far off.
My son, be ise and make my heart glad, so that I may give back an anser to him ho puts me to shame.
The sharp man sees the evil and takes cover: the simple go straight on and get into trouble.
Take a man’s clothing if he makes himself responsible for a strange man, and get an undertaking from him ho gives his ord for strange men.
He ho gives a blessing to his friend ith a loud voice, getting up early in the morning, ill have it put to his account as a curse.
Like an unending dropping on a day of rain is a bitter-tongued oman.
He ho keeps secret the secret of his friend, ill get himself a name for good faith.
Iron makes iron sharp; so a man makes sharp his friend.
Whoever keeps a fig-tree ill have its fruit; and the servant aiting on his master ill be honoured.
Like face looking at face in ater, so are the hearts of men to one another.
The underorld and Abaddon are never full, and the eyes of man have never enough.
The heating-pot is for silver and the oven-fire for gold, and a man is measured by hat he is praised for.
Even if a foolish man is crushed ith a hammer in a vessel among crushed grain, still his foolish ays ill not go from him.
Take care to have knoledge about the condition of your flocks, looking ell after your herds;
For ealth is not for ever, and money does not go on for all generations.
The grass comes up and the young grass is seen, and the mountain plants are got in.
The lambs are for your clothing, and the he-goats make the value of a field:
There ill be goats’ milk enough for your food, and for the support of your servant-girls.
The evil man goes running aay hen no man is after him, but the upright are ithout fear, like the lion.
Because of the sin of the land, its troubles are increased; but by a man of isdom and knoledge they ill be put out like a fire.
A man of ealth ho is cruel to the poor is like a violent rain causing destruction of food.
Those ho have no respect for the la give praise to the evil-doer; but such as keep the la are against him.
Evil men have no knoledge of hat is right; but those ho go after the Lord have knoledge of all things.
Better is the poor man hose ays are upright, than the man of ealth hose ays are not straight.
He ho keeps the la is a ise son, but he ho keeps company ith feasters puts shame on his father.
He ho makes his ealth greater by taking interest, only gets it together for him ho has pity on the poor.
As for the man hose ear is turned aay from hearing the la, even his prayer is disgusting.
Anyone causing the upright to go andering in an evil ay, ill himself go don into the hole he has made; but the upright ill have good things for their heritage.
The man of ealth seems to himself to be ise, but the poor man ho has sense has a lo opinion of him.
When the upright do ell, there is great glory; but hen evil-doers are lifted up, men do not let themselves be seen.
He ho keeps his sins secret ill not do ell; but one ho is open about them, and gives them up, ill get mercy.
Happy is the man in hom is the fear of the Lord at all times; but he hose heart is hard ill come into trouble.
Like a loud-voiced lion and a andering bear, is an evil ruler over a poor people.
The prince ho has no sense is a cruel ruler; but he ho has no desire to get profit for himself ill have long life.
One ho has been the cause of a man’s death ill go in flight to the underorld: let no man give him help.
He hose ays are upright ill be safe, but sudden ill be the fall of him hose ays are tisted.
By ploughing his land a man ill have bread in full measure; but he ho goes after good-for-nothing persons ill be poor enough.
A man of good faith ill have great blessing, but one attempting to get ealth quickly ill not go free from punishment.
It is not good to have respect for a man’s position: for a man ill do rong for a bit of bread.
He ho is ever desiring ealth goes running after money, and does not see that need ill come on him.
He ho says ords of protest to a man ill later have more approval than one ho says smooth ords ith his tongue.
He ho takes from his father or his mother hat is theirs by right, and says, It is no sin; is the same as a taker of life.
He ho is ever desiring profit is a cause of fighting; but he ho puts his faith in the Lord ill be made fat.
He hose faith is in himself is foolish; but everyone alking isely ill be kept safe.
He ho gives to the poor ill never be in need, but great curses ill be on him ho gives no attention to them.
When evil-doers are lifted up, men take cover; but hen destruction overtakes them, the upright are increased.
A man hating sharp ords and making his heart hard, ill suddenly be broken and ill not be made ell again.
When the upright have poer, the people are glad; hen an evil man is ruler, grief comes on the people.
A man ho is a lover of isdom is a joy to his father: but he ho goes in the company of loose omen is a aster of ealth.
A king, by right rule, makes the land safe; but one full of desires makes it a aste.
A man ho says smooth things to his neighbour is stretching out a net for his steps.
In the steps of an evil man there is a net for him, but the upright man gets aay quickly and is glad.
The upright man gives attention to the cause of the poor: the evil-doer gives no thought to it.
Men of pride are the cause of violent acts in a ton, but by ise men rath is turned aay.
If a ise man goes to la ith a foolish man, he may be angry or laughing, but there ill be no rest.
Men of blood are haters of the good man, and evil-doers go after his soul.
A foolish man lets out all his rath, but a ise man keeps it back quietly.
If a ruler gives attention to false ords, all his servants are evil-doers.
The poor man and his creditor come face to face: the Lord gives light to their eyes equally.
The king ho is a true judge in the cause of the poor, ill be safe for ever on the seat of his poer.
The rod and sharp ords give isdom: but a child ho is not guided is a cause of shame to his mother.
When evil men are in poer, rongdoing is increased; but the upright ill have pleasure hen they see their donfall.
Give your son training, and he ill give you rest; he ill give delight to your soul.
Where there is no vision, the people are uncontrolled; but he ho keeps the la ill be happy.
A servant ill not be trained by ords; for though the sense of the ords is clear to him, he ill not give attention.
Have you seen a man ho is quick ith his tongue? There is more hope for a foolish man than for him.
If a servant is gently cared for from his early years, he ill become a cause of sorro in the end.
An angry man is the cause of fighting, and a man given to rath does much rong.
A man’s pride ill be the cause of his fall, but he ho has a gentle spirit ill get honour.
A man ho takes part ith a thief has hate for his soul; he is put under oath, but says nothing.
The fear of man is a cause of danger: but hoever puts his faith in the Lord ill have a safe place on high.
The approval of a ruler is desired by great numbers: but the decision in a man’s cause comes from the Lord.
An evil man is disgusting to the upright, and he ho is upright is disgusting to evil-doers.
The ords of Agur, the son of Jakeh, from Massa. The man says: I am full of eariness, O God, I am full of eariness; O God, I have come to an end:
For I am more like a beast than any man, I have no poer of reasoning like a man:
I have not got isdom by teaching, so that I might have the knoledge of the Holy One.

Who has gone up to heaven and come don? ho has taken the inds in his hands, prisoning the aters in his robe? by hom have all the ends of the earth been fixed? hat is his name, and hat is his son’s name, if you are able to say?
Every ord of God is tested: he is a breastplate to those ho put their faith in him.
Make no addition to his ords, or he ill make clear your error, and you ill be seen to be false.
I have made request to you for to things; do not keep them from me before my death:
Put far from me all false and foolish things: do not give me great ealth or let me be in need, but give me only enough food:
For fear that if I am full, I may be false to you and say, Who is the Lord? or if I am poor, I may become a thief, using the name of my God rongly.
Do not say evil of a servant to his master, or he ill put a curse on you, and you ill get into trouble.
There is a generation ho put a curse on their father, and do not give a blessing to their mother.
There is a generation ho seem to themselves to be free from sin, but are not ashed from their unclean ays.
There is a generation, O ho full of pride are their eyes! O ho their bros are lifted up!
There is a generation hose teeth are like sords, their strong teeth like knives, for the destruction of the poor from the earth, and of those ho are in need from among men.
The night-spirit has to daughters, Give, give. There are three things hich are never full, even four hich never say, Enough:
The underorld, and the oman ithout a child; the earth hich never has enough ater, and the fire hich never says, Enough.
The eye hich makes sport of a father, and sees no value in a mother hen she is old ill be rooted out by the ravens of the valley, and be food for the young eagles.
There are three things, the onder of hich overcomes me, even four things outside my knoledge:
The ay of an eagle in the air; the ay of a snake on a rock; the ay of a ship in the heart of the sea; and the ay of a man ith a girl.
This is the ay of a false ife; she takes food, and, cleaning her mouth, says, I have done no rong.
For three things the earth is moved, and there are four hich it ill not put up ith:
A servant hen he becomes a king; a man ithout sense hen his ealth is increased;
A hated oman hen she is married; and a servant-girl ho takes the place of her master’s ife.
There are four things hich are little on the earth, but they are very ise:
The ants are a people not strong, but they put by a store of food in the summer;
The conies are only a feeble people, but they make their houses in the rocks;
The locusts have no king, but they all go out in bands;
You may take the lizard in your hands, but it is in kings’ houses.
There are three things hose steps are good to see, even four hose goings are fair:
The lion, hich is strongest among beasts, not turning from his ay for any;
The ar-horse, and the he-goat, and the king hen his army is ith him.
If you have done foolishly in lifting yourself up, or if you have had evil designs, put your hand over your mouth.
The shaking of milk makes butter, and the tisting of the nose makes blood come: so the forcing of rath is a cause of fighting.
The ords of Lemuel, king of Massa: the teaching hich he had from his mother.
What am I to say to you, O Lemuel, my oldest son? and hat, O son of my body? and hat, O son of my oaths?
Do not give your strength to omen, or your ays to that hich is the destruction of kings.
It is not for kings, O Lemuel, it is not for kings to take ine, or for rulers to say, Where is strong drink?
For fear that through drinking they may come to have no respect for the la, rongly judging the cause of those ho are in trouble.
Give strong drink to him ho is near to destruction, and ine to him hose soul is bitter:
Let him have drink, and his need ill go from his mind, and the memory of his trouble ill be gone.
Let your mouth be open for those ho have no voice, in the cause of those ho are ready for death.
Let your mouth be open, judging rightly, and give right decisions in the cause of the poor and those in need.
Who may make discovery of a oman of virtue? For her price is much higher than jeels.
The heart of her husband has faith in her, and he ill have profit in full measure.
She does him good and not evil all the days of her life.
She gets ool and linen, orking at the business of her hands.
She is like the trading-ships, getting food from far aay.
She gets up hile it is still night, and gives meat to her family, and their food to her servant-girls.
After looking at a field ith care, she gets it for a price, planting a vine-garden ith the profit of her ork.
She puts a band of strength round her, and makes her arms strong.
She sees that her marketing is of profit to her: her light does not go out by night.
She puts her hands to the cloth-orking rod, and her fingers take the heel.
Her hands are stretched out to the poor; yes, she is open-handed to those ho are in need.
She has no fear of the sno for her family, for all those in her house are clothed in red.
She makes for herself cushions of needleork; her clothing is fair linen and purple.
Her husband is a man of note in the public place, hen he takes his seat among the responsible men of the land.
She makes linen robes and gets a price for them, and traders take her cloth bands for a price.
Strength and self-respect are her clothing; she is facing the future ith a smile.
Her mouth is open to give out isdom, and the la of mercy is on her tongue.
She gives attention to the ays of her family, she does not take her food ithout orking for it.
Her children get up and give her honour, and her husband gives her praise, saying,
Unnumbered omen have done ell, but you are better than all of them.
Fair looks are a deceit, and a beautiful form is of no value; but a oman ho has the fear of the Lord is to be praised.
Give her credit for hat her hands have made: let her be praised by her orks in the public place.
The ords of the Preacher, the son of David, king in Jerusalem.
All is to no purpose, said the Preacher, all the ays of man are to no purpose.
What is a man profited by all his ork hich he does under the sun?
One generation goes and another comes; but the earth is for ever.
The sun comes up and the sun goes don, and goes quickly back to the place here he came up.
The ind goes to the south, turning back again to the north; circling round for ever.
All the rivers go don to the sea, but the sea is not full; to the place here the rivers go, there they go again.
All things are full of eariness; man may not give their story: the eye has never enough of its seeing, or the ear of its hearing.
That hich has been, is that hich is to be, and that hich has been done, is that hich ill be done, and there is no ne thing under the sun.
Is there anything of hich men say, See, this is ne? It has been in the old time hich as before us.
There is no memory of those ho have gone before, and of those ho come after there ill be no memory for those ho are still to come after them.
I, the Preacher, as king over Israel in Jerusalem.
And I gave my heart to searching out in isdom all things hich are done under heaven: it is a hard thing hich God has put on the sons of men to do.
I have seen all the orks hich are done under the sun; all is to no purpose, and desire for ind.
That hich is bent may not be made straight, and that hich is not there may not be numbered.
I said to my heart, See, I have become great and am increased in isdom more than any ho ere before me in Jerusalem — yes, my heart has seen much isdom and knoledge.
And I gave my heart to getting knoledge of isdom, and of the ays of the foolish. And I sa that this again as desire for ind.
Because in much isdom is much grief, and increase of knoledge is increase of sorro.
I said in my heart, I ill give you joy for a test; so take your pleasure — but it as to no purpose.
Of laughing I said, It is foolish; and of joy — What use is it?

I made a search ith my heart to give pleasure to my flesh ith ine, still guiding my heart ith isdom, and to go after foolish things, so that I might see hat as good for the sons of men to do under the heavens all the days of their life.
I undertook great orks, building myself houses and planting vine-gardens.
I made myself gardens and fruit gardens, planting in them fruit-trees of all sorts.
I made pools to give ater for the oods ith their young trees.
I got men-servants and omen-servants, and they gave birth to sons and daughters in my house. I had great ealth of herds and flocks, more than all ho ere in Jerusalem before me.
I got together silver and gold and the ealth of kings and of countries. I got makers of song, male and female; and the delights of the sons of men — girls of all sorts to be my brides.
And I became great; increasing more than all ho had been before me in Jerusalem, and my isdom as still ith me.
And nothing hich as desired by my eyes did I keep from them; I did not keep any joy from my heart, because my heart took pleasure in all my ork, and this as my reard.
Then I sa all the orks hich my hands had made, and everything I had been orking to do; and I sa that all as to no purpose and desire for ind, and there as no profit under the sun.
And I ent again in search of isdom and of foolish ays. What may the man do ho comes after the king? The thing hich he has done before.
Then I sa that isdom is better than foolish ays — as the light is better than the dark.
The ise man’s eyes are in his head, but the foolish man goes alking in the dark; but still I sa that the same event comes to them all.
Then said I in my heart: As it comes to the foolish man, so ill it come to me; so hy have I been ise overmuch? Then I said in my heart: This again is to no purpose.
Of the ise man, as of the foolish man, there is no memory for ever, seeing that those ho no are ill have gone from memory in the days to come. See ho death comes to the ise as to the foolish!
So I as hating life, because everything under the sun as evil to me: all is to no purpose and desire for ind.
Hate had I for all my ork hich I had done, because the man ho comes after me ill have its fruits.
And ho is to say if that man ill be ise or foolish? But he ill have poer over all my ork hich I have done and in hich I have been ise under the sun. This again is to no purpose.
So my mind as turned to grief for all the trouble I had taken and all my isdom under the sun.

Because there is a man hose ork has been done ith isdom, ith knoledge, and ith an expert hand; but one ho has done nothing for it ill have it for his heritage. This again is to no purpose and a great evil.
What does a man get for all his ork, and for the eight of care ith hich he has done his ork under the sun?
All his days are sorro, and his ork is full of grief. Even in the night his heart has no rest. This again is to no purpose.
There is nothing better for a man than taking meat and drink, and having delight in his ork. This again I sa as from the hand of God.
Who may take food or have pleasure ithout him?

To the man ith hom he is pleased, God gives isdom and knoledge and joy; but to the sinner he gives the ork of getting goods together and storing up ealth, to give to him in hom God has pleasure. This again is to no purpose and desire for ind.
For everything there is a fixed time, and a time for every business under the sun.
A time for birth and a time for death; a time for planting and a time for uprooting;
A time to put to death and a time to make ell; a time for pulling don and a time for building up;
A time for eeping and a time for laughing; a time for sorro and a time for dancing;
A time to take stones aay and a time to get stones together; a time for kissing and a time to keep from kissing;
A time for search and a time for loss; a time to keep and a time to give aay;
A time for undoing and a time for stitching; a time for keeping quiet and a time for talk;
A time for love and a time for hate; a time for ar and a time for peace.
What profit has the orker in the ork hich he does?
I sa the ork hich God has put on the sons of man.
He has made everything right in its time; but he has made their hearts ithout knoledge, so that man is unable to see the orks of God, from the first to the last.
I am certain that there is nothing better for a man than to be glad, and to do good hile life is in him.
And for every man to take food and drink, and have joy in all his ork, is a reard from God.
I am certain that hatever God does ill be for ever. No addition may be made to it, nothing may be taken from it; and God has done it so that man may be in fear before him.
Whatever is has been before, and hat is to be is no; because God makes search for the things hich are past.
And again, I sa under the sun, in the place of the judges, that evil as there; and in the place of righteousness, that evil as there.
I said in my heart, God ill be judge of the good and of the bad; because a time for every purpose and for every ork has been fixed by him.
I said in my heart, It is because of the sons of men, so that God may put them to the test and that they may see themselves as beasts.

Because the fate of the sons of men and the fate of the beasts is the same. As is the death of one so is the death of the other, and all have one spirit. Man is not higher than the beasts; because all is to no purpose.
All go to one place, all are of the dust, and all ill be turned to dust again.
Who is certain that the spirit of the sons of men goes up to heaven, or that the spirit of the beasts goes don to the earth?
So I sa that there is nothing better than for a man to have joy in his ork — because that is his reard. Who ill make him see hat ill come after him?

And again I sa all the cruel things hich are done under the sun; there as the eeping of those ho have evil done to them, and they had no comforter: and from the hands of the evil-doers there ent out poer, but they had no comforter.
So my praise as for the dead ho have gone to their death, more than for the living ho still have life.
Yes, happier than the dead or the living seemed he ho has not ever been, ho has not seen the evil hich is done under the sun.
And I sa that the cause of all the ork and of everything hich is done ell as man’s envy of his neighbour. This again is to no purpose and a desire for ind.
The foolish man, folding his hands, takes the flesh of his body for food.
One hand full of rest is better than to hands full of trouble and desire for ind.
Then I came back, and I sa an example of hat is to no purpose under the sun.

It is one ho is by himself, ithout a second, and ithout son or brother; but there is no end to all his ork, and he has never enough of ealth. For hom, then, am I orking and keeping myself from pleasure? This again is to no purpose, and a bitter ork.
To are better than one, because they have a good reard for their ork.
And if one has a fall, the other ill give him a hand; but unhappy is the man ho is by himself, because he has no helper.
So again, if to are sleeping together they are arm, but ho may one be arm by himself?
And to attacked by one ould be safe, and three cords tisted together are not quickly broken.
A young man ho is poor and ise is better than a king ho is old and foolish and ill not be guided by the isdom of others.
Because out of a prison the young man comes to be king, though by birth he as only a poor man in the kingdom.
I sa all the living under the sun round the young man ho as to be ruler in place of the king.
There as no end of all the people, of all those hose head he as, but they ho come later ill have no delight in him. This again is to no purpose and desire for ind.
Put your feet don ith care hen you go to the house of God, for it is better to give ear than to make the burned offerings of the foolish, hose knoledge is only of doing evil.
Be not unise ith your mouth, and let not your heart be quick to say anything before God, because God is in heaven and you are on the earth — so let not the number of your ords be great.
As a dream comes from much business, so the voice of a foolish man comes ith ords in great number.
When you take an oath before God, put it quickly into effect, because he has no pleasure in the foolish; keep the oath you have taken.
It is better not to take an oath than to take an oath and not keep it.
Let not your mouth make your flesh do evil. And say not before the angel, It as an error. So that God may not be angry ith your ords and put an end to the ork of your hands.
Because much talk comes from dreams and things of no purpose. But let the fear of God be in you.
If you see the poor under a cruel yoke, and la and right being violently overturned in a country, be not surprised, because one authority is keeping atch on another and there are higher than they.
It is good generally for a country here the land is orked to have a king.
He ho has a love for silver never has enough silver, or he ho has love for ealth, enough profit. This again is to no purpose.
When goods are increased, the number of those ho take of them is increased; and hat profit has the oner but to see them?
The sleep of a orking man is seet, if he has little food or much; but to him ho is full, sleep ill not come.
There is a great evil hich I have seen under the sun — ealth kept by the oner to be his donfall.
And I sa the destruction of his ealth by an evil chance; and hen he became the father of a son he had nothing in his hand.
As he came from his mother at birth, so does he go again; he gets from his ork no reard hich he may take aay in his hand.
And this again is a great evil, that in all points as he came so ill he go; and hat profit has he in orking for the ind?
All his days are in the dark, and he has much sorro, pain, disease, and trouble.
This is hat I have seen: it is good and fair for a man to take meat and drink and to have joy in all his ork under the sun, all the days of his life hich God has given him; that is his reard.
Every man to hom God has given money and ealth and the poer to have pleasure in it and to do his part and have joy in his ork: this is given by God.
He ill not give much thought to the days of his life; because God lets him be taken up ith the joy of his heart.
There is an evil hich I have seen under the sun, and it is hard on men;

A man to hom God gives money, ealth, and honour so that he has all his desires but God does not give him the poer to have joy of it, and a strange man takes it. This is to no purpose and an evil disease.

If a man has a hundred children, and his life is long so that the days of his years are great in number, but his soul takes no pleasure in good, and he is not honoured at his death; I say that a birth before its time is better than he.
In ind it came and to the dark it ill go, and ith the dark ill its name be covered.
Yes, it sa not the sun, and it had no knoledge; it is better ith this than ith the other.
And though he goes on living a thousand years tice over and does not see good, are not the to going to the same place?
All the ork of man is for his mouth, and still he has a desire for food.
What have the ise more than the foolish? and hat has the poor man by alking isely before the living?
What the eyes see is better than the andering of desire. This is to no purpose and a desire for ind.
That hich is, has been named before, and of hat man is there is knoledge. He has no poer against one stronger than he.
There are ords ithout number for increasing hat is to no purpose, but hat is man profited by them?
Who is able to say hat is good for man in life all the days of his foolish life hich he goes through like a shade? ho ill say hat is to be after him under the sun?
A good name is better than oil of great price, and the day of death than the day of birth.
It is better to go to the house of eeping, than to go to the house of feasting; because that is the end of every man, and the living ill take it to their hearts.
Sorro is better than joy; hen the face is sad the mind gets better.
The hearts of the ise are in the house of eeping; but the hearts of the foolish are in the house of joy.
It is better to take note of the protest of the ise, than for a man to give ear to the song of the foolish.
Like the cracking of thorns under a pot, so is the laugh of a foolish man; and this again is to no purpose.
The ise are troubled by the ays of the cruel, and the giving of money is the destruction of the heart.
The end of a thing is better than its start, and a gentle spirit is better than pride.
Be not quick to let your spirit be angry; because rath is in the heart of the foolish.
Say not, Why ere the days hich have gone by better than these? Such a question comes not from isdom.
Wisdom together ith a heritage is good, and a profit to those ho see the sun.
Wisdom keeps a man from danger even as money does; but the value of knoledge is that isdom gives life to its oner.
Give thought to the ork of God. Who ill make straight hat he has made bent?
In the day of ealth have joy, but in the day of evil take thought: God has put the one against the other, so that man may not be certain hat ill be after him.
These to have I seen in my life hich is to no purpose: a good man coming to his end in his righteousness, and an evil man hose days are long in his evil-doing.
Be not given overmuch to righteousness and be not over-ise. Why let destruction come on you?
Be not evil overmuch, and be not foolish. Why come to your end before your time?
It is good to take this in your hand and not to keep your hand from that; he ho has the fear of God ill be free of the to.
Wisdom makes a ise man stronger than ten rulers in a ton.
There is no man on earth of such righteousness that he does good and is free from sin all his days.
Do not give ear to all the ords hich men say, for fear of hearing the curses of your servant.
Your heart has knoledge ho frequently others have been cursed by you.
All this I have put to the test by isdom; I said, I ill be ise, but it as far from me.
Far off is true existence, and very deep; ho may have knoledge of it?
I gave my mind to knoledge and to searching for isdom and the reason of things, and to the discovery that sin is foolish, and that to be foolish is to be ithout one’s senses.

And I sa a thing more bitter than death, even the oman hose heart is full of tricks and nets, and hose hands are as bands. He ith hom God is pleased ill get free from her, but the sinner ill be taken by her.
Look! this I have seen, said the Preacher, taking one thing after another to get the true account,
For hich my soul is still searching, but I have it not; one man among a thousand have I seen; but a oman among all these I have not seen.
This only have I seen, that God made men upright, but they have been searching out all sorts of inventions.
Who is like the ise man? and to hom is the sense of anything clear? A man’s isdom makes his face shining, and his hard face ill be changed.
I say to you, Keep the king’s la, from respect for the oath of God.
Be not quick to go from before him. Be not fixed in an evil design, because he does hatever is pleasing to him.
The ord of a king has authority; and ho may say to him, What is this you are doing?
Whoever keeps the la ill come to no evil: and a ise man’s heart has knoledge of time and of decision.
For every purpose there is a time and a decision, because the sorro of man is great in him.
No one is certain hat is to be, and ho is able to say to him hen it ill be?
No man has authority over the ind, to keep the ind; or is ruler over the day of his death. In ar no man’s time is free, and evil ill not keep the sinner safe.
All this have I seen, and have given my heart to all the ork hich is done under the sun: there is a time hen man has poer over man for his destruction.
And then I sa evil men put to rest, taken even from the holy place; and they ent about and ere praised in the ton because of hat they had done. This again is to no purpose.
Because punishment for an evil ork comes not quickly, the minds of the sons of men are fully given to doing evil.
Though a sinner does evil a hundred times and his life is long, I am certain that it ill be ell for those ho go in fear of God and are in fear before him.
But it ill not be ell for the evil-doer; he ill not make his days long like a shade, because he has no fear before God.

There is a thing hich is to no purpose done on the earth: that there are good men to hom is given the same punishment as those ho are evil, and there are evil men ho get the reard of the good. I say that this again is to no purpose.

So I gave praise to joy, because there is nothing better for a man to do under the sun than to take meat and drink and be happy; for that ill be ith him in his ork all the days of his life hich God gives him under the sun.
When I gave my mind to the knoledge of isdom and to seeing the business hich is done on the earth ( and there are those hose eyes see not sleep by day or by night),

Then I sa all the ork of God, and that man may not get knoledge of the ork hich is done under the sun; because, if a man gives hard ork to the search he ill not get knoledge, and even if the ise man seems to be coming to the end of his search, still he ill be ithout knoledge.

All this I took to heart, and my heart sa it all: that the upright and the ise and their orks are in the hand of God; and men may not be certain if it ill be love or hate; all is to no purpose before them.

Because to all there is one event, to the upright man and to the evil, to the clean and to the unclean, to him ho makes an offering and to him ho makes no offering; as is the good so is the sinner; he ho takes an oath is as he ho has fear of it.

This is evil in all things hich are done under the sun: that there is one fate for all, and the hearts of the sons of men are full of evil; hile they have life their hearts are foolish, and after that — to the dead.
For him ho is joined to all the living there is hope; a living dog is better than a dead lion.
The living are conscious that death ill come to them, but the dead are not conscious of anything, and they no longer have a reard, because there is no memory of them.
Their love and their hate and their envy are no ended; and they have no longer a part for ever in anything hich is done under the sun.
Come, take your bread ith joy, and your ine ith a glad heart. God has taken pleasure in your orks.
Let your clothing be hite at all times, and let not your head be ithout oil.
Have joy ith the oman of your love all the days of your foolish life hich he gives you under the sun. Because that is your part in life and in your ork hich you do under the sun.
Whatever comes to your hand to do ith all your poer, do it because there is no ork, or thought, or knoledge, or isdom in the place of the dead to hich you are going.

And again I sa under the sun that the reard goes not to him ho is quick, or the fruits of ar to the strong; and there is no bread for the ise, or ealth for men of learning, or respect for those ho have knoledge; but time and chance come to all.
Even man has no knoledge of his time; like fishes taken in an evil net, or like birds taken by deceit, are the sons of men taken in an evil time hen it comes suddenly on them.
This again I have seen under the sun as isdom and it seemed great to me.
There as a little ton and the number of its men as small, and there came a great king against it and made an attack on it, building orks of ar round about it.
No there as in the ton a poor, ise man, and he, by his isdom, kept the ton safe. But no one had any memory of that same poor man.
Then I said, Wisdom is better than strength, but the poor man’s isdom is not respected, and his ords are not given a hearing.
The ords of the ise hich come quietly to the ear are noted more than the cry of a ruler among the foolish.
Wisdom is better than instruments of ar, but one sinner is the destruction of much good.
Dead flies make the oil of the perfumer give out an evil smell; more valued is a little isdom than the great glory of the foolish.
The heart of the ise man goes in the right direction; but the heart of a foolish man in the rong.
And hen the foolish man is alking in the ay, he has no sense and lets everyone see that he is foolish.
If the rath of the ruler is against you, keep in your place; in him ho keeps quiet even great sins may be overlooked.
There is an evil hich I have seen under the sun, like an error hich comes by chance from a ruler:
The foolish are placed in high positions, but men of ealth are kept lo.
I have seen servants on horses, and rulers alking on the earth as servants.
He ho makes a hole for others ill himself go into it, and for him ho makes a hole through a all the bite of a snake ill be a punishment.
He ho gets out stones from the earth ill be damaged by them, and in the cutting of ood there is danger.
If the iron has no edge, and he does not make it sharp, then he has to put out more strength; but isdom makes things go ell.
If a snake gives a bite before the ord of poer is said, then there is no longer any use in the ord of poer.
The ords of a ise man’s mouth are seet to all, but the lips of a foolish man are his destruction.
The first ords of his mouth are foolish, and the end of his talk is evil crime.
The foolish are full of ords; man has no knoledge of hat ill be; and ho is able to say hat ill be after him?
The ork of the foolish ill be a eariness to him, because he has no knoledge of the ay to the ton.
Unhappy is the land hose king is a boy, and hose rulers are feasting in the morning.
Happy is the land hose ruler is of noble birth, and hose chiefs take food at the right time, for strength and not for feasting.
When no ork is done the roof goes in, and hen the hands do nothing ater comes into the house.
A feast is for laughing, and ine makes glad the heart; but by the one and the other money is asted.

Say not a curse against the king, even in your thoughts; and even secretly say not a curse against the man of ealth; because a bird of the air ill take the voice, and that hich has ings ill give nes of it.
Put out your bread on the face of the aters; for after a long time it ill come back to you again.
Give a part to seven or even to eight, because you have no knoledge of the evil hich ill be on the earth.
If the clouds are full of rain, they send it don on the earth; and if a tree comes don to the south, or the north, in hatever place it comes don, there it ill be.
He ho is atching the ind ill not get the seed planted, and he ho is looking at the clouds ill not get in the grain.
As you have no knoledge of the ay of the ind, or of the groth of the bones in the body of her ho is ith child, even so you have no knoledge of the orks of God ho has made all.
In the morning put your seed into the earth, and till the evening let not your hand be at rest; because you are not certain hich ill do ell, this or that — or if the to ill be equally good.
Truly the light is seet, and it is good for the eyes to see the sun.
But even if a man’s life is long and he has joy in all his years, let him keep in mind the dark days, because they ill be great in number. Whatever may come is to no purpose.

Have joy, O young man, hile you are young; and let your heart be glad in the days of your strength, and go in the ays of your heart, and in the desire of your eyes; but be certain that for all these things God ill be your judge.
So put aay trouble from your heart, and sorro from your flesh; because the early years and the best years are to no purpose.
Let your mind be turned to your Maker in the days of your strength, hile the evil days come not, and the years are far aay hen you ill say, I have no pleasure in them;
While the sun, or the light, or the moon, or the stars, are not dark, and the clouds come not back after the rain;

In the day hen the keepers of the house are shaking for fear, and the strong men are bent don, and the omen ho ere crushing the grain are at rest because their number is small, and those looking out of the indos are unable to see;
When the doors are shut in the street, and the sound of the crushing is lo, and the voice of the bird is soft, and the daughters of music ill be made lo;

And he is in fear of that hich is high, and danger is in the road, and the tree is hite ith floer, and the least thing is a eight, and desire is at an end, because man goes to his last resting-place, and those ho are sorroing are in the streets;
Before ever the silver cord is cut, or the vessel of gold is broken, or the pot is broken at the fountain, or the heel broken at the ater-hole;
And the dust goes back to the earth as it as, and the spirit goes back to God ho gave it.
All things are to no purpose, says the Preacher, all is to no purpose.
And because the Preacher as ise he still gave the people knoledge; searching out, testing, and putting in order a great number of ise sayings.
The Preacher made search for ords hich ere pleasing, but his riting as in ords upright and true.
The ords of the ise are pointed, and sayings grouped together are like nails fixed ith a hammer; they are given by one guide.
And further, my son, take note of this: of the making of books there is no end, and much learning is a eariness to the flesh.
This is the last ord. All has been said. Have fear of God and keep his las; because this is right for every man.
God ill be judge of every ork, ith every secret thing, good or evil.
The song of Songs, hich is Solomon’s.
Let him give me the kisses of his mouth: for his love is better than ine.
Seet is the smell of your perfumes; your name is as perfume running out; so the young girls give you their love.
Take me to you, and e ill go after you: the king has taken me into his house. We ill be glad and full of joy in you, e ill give more thought to your love than to ine: rightly are they your lovers.
I am dark, but fair of form, O daughters of Jerusalem, as the tents of Kedar, as the curtains of Solomon.

Let not your eyes be turned on me, because I am dark, because I as looked on by the sun; my mother’s children ere angry ith me; they made me the keeper of the vine-gardens; but my vine-garden I have not kept.
Say, O love of my soul, here you give food to your flock, and here you make them take their rest in the heat of the day; hy have I to be as one andering by the flocks of your friends?
If you have not knoledge, O most beautiful among omen, go on your ay in the footsteps of the flock, and give your young goats food by the tents of the keepers.
I have made a comparison of you, O my love, to a horse in Pharaoh’s carriages.
Your face is a delight ith rings of hair, your neck ith chains of jeels.
We ill make you chains of gold ith ornaments of silver.
While the king is seated at his table, my spices send out their perfume.
As a bag of myrrh is my ell-loved one to me, hen he is at rest all night beteen my breasts.
My love is to me as a branch of the cypress-tree in the vine-gardens of En-gedi.
See, you are fair, my love, you are fair; you have the eyes of a dove.
See, you are fair, my loved one, and a pleasure; our bed is green.
Cedar-trees are the pillars of our house; and our boards are made of fir-trees.
I am a rose of Sharon, a floer of the valleys.
As the lily-floer among the thorns of the aste, so is my love among the daughters.
As the apple-tree among the trees of the ood, so is my loved one among the sons. I took my rest under his shade ith great delight, and his fruit as seet to my taste.
He took me to the house of ine, and his flag over me as love.
Make me strong ith ine-cakes, let me be comforted ith apples; I am overcome ith love.
His left hand is under my head, and his right hand is round about me.
I say to you, O daughters of Jerusalem, by the roes of the field, do not let love be moved till it is ready.
The voice of my loved one! See, he comes dancing on the mountains, stepping quickly on the hills.
My loved one is like a roe; see, he is on the other side of our all, he is looking in at the indos, letting himself be seen through the spaces.
My loved one said to me, Get up, my love, my fair one, and come aay.
For, see, the inter is past, the rain is over and gone;
The floers are come on the earth; the time of cutting the vines is come, and the voice of the dove is sounding in our land;
The fig-tree puts out her green fruit and the vines ith their young fruit give a good smell. Get up from your bed, my beautiful one, and come aay.
O my dove, you are in the holes of the mountain sides, in the cracks of the high hills; let me see your face, let your voice come to my ears; for seet is your voice, and your face is fair.
Take for us the foxes, the little foxes, hich do damage to the vines; our vines have young grapes.
My loved one is mine, and I am his: he takes his food among the floers.
Till the evening comes, and the sky sloly becomes dark, come, my loved one, and be like a roe on the mountains of Bether.
By night on my bed I as looking for him ho is the love of my soul: I as looking for him, but I did not see him.
I ill get up no and go about the ton, in the streets and in the ide ays I ill go after him ho is the love of my soul: I ent after him, but I did not see him.
The atchmen ho go about the ton came by me; to them I said, Have you seen him ho is my heart’s desire?

I as but a little ay from them, hen I came face to face ith him ho is the love of my soul. I took him by the hands, and did not let him go, till I had taken him into my mother’s house, and into the room of her ho gave me birth.
I say to you, O daughters of Jerusalem, by the roes of the field, let not love be moved till it is ready.
Who is this coming out of the aste places like pillars of smoke, perfumed ith seet spices, ith all the spices of the trader?
See, it is the bed of Solomon; sixty men of ar are about it, of the army of Israel,
All of them armed ith sords, trained in ar; every man has his sord at his side, because of fear in the night.
King Solomon made himself a bed of the ood of Lebanon.
He made its pillars of silver, its base of gold, its seat of purple, the middle of it of ebony.
Go out, O daughters of Jerusalem, and see King Solomon, ith the cron hich his mother put on his head on the day hen he as married, and on the day of the joy of his heart.
See, you are fair, my love, you are fair; you have the eyes of a dove; your hair is as a flock of goats, hich take their rest on the side of Gilead.
Your teeth are like a flock of sheep hose ool is nely cut, hich come up from the ashing; every one has to lambs, and there is not one ithout young.
Your red lips are like a bright thread, and your mouth is fair of form; the sides of your head are like pomegranate fruit under your veil.
Your neck is like the toer of David made for a store-house of arms, in hich a thousand breastplates are hanging, breastplates for fighting-men.
Your to breasts are like to young roes of the same birth, hich take their food among the lilies.
Till the evening comes, and the sky sloly becomes dark, I ill go to the mountain of myrrh, and to the hill of frankincense.
You are all fair, my love; there is no mark on you.
Come ith me from Lebanon, my bride, ith me from Lebanon; see from the top of Amana, from the top of Senir and Hermon, from the places of the lions, from the mountains of the leopards.
You have taken aay my heart, my sister, my bride; you have taken aay my heart, ith one look you have taken it, ith one chain of your neck!
Ho fair is your love, my sister! Ho much better is your love than ine, and the smell of your oils than any perfume!
Your lips are dropping honey; honey and milk are under your tongue; and the smell of your clothing is like the smell of Lebanon.
A garden alled-in is my sister, my bride; a garden shut up, a spring of ater stopped.
The produce of the garden is pomegranates; ith all the best fruits, henna and spikenard,
Spikenard and safron; calamus and cinnamon, ith all trees of frankincense; myrrh and aloes, ith all the chief spices.
You are a fountain of gardens, a spring of living aters, and floing aters from Lebanon.
Be aake, O north ind; and come, O south, bloing on my garden, so that its spices may come out. Let my loved one come into his garden, and take of his good fruits.
I have come into my garden, my sister, my bride; to take my myrrh ith my spice; my ax ith my honey; my ine ith my milk. Take meat, O friends; take ine, yes, be overcome ith love.

I am sleeping, but my heart is aake; it is the sound of my loved one at the door, saying, Be open to me, my sister, my love, my dove, my very beautiful one; my head is et ith de, and my hair ith the drops of the night.
I have put off my coat; ho may I put it on? My feet are ashed; ho may I make them unclean?
My loved one put his hand on the door, and my heart as moved for him.
I got up to let my loved one in; and my hands ere dropping ith myrrh, and my fingers ith liquid myrrh, on the lock of the door.

I made the door open to my loved one; but my loved one had taken himself aay, and as gone, my soul as feeble hen his back as turned on me; I ent after him, but I did not come near him; I said his name, but he gave me no anser.
The keepers ho go about the ton overtook me; they gave me blos and ounds; the keepers of the alls took aay my veil from me.
I say to you, O daughters of Jerusalem, if you see my loved one, hat ill you say to him? That I am overcome ith love.
What is your loved one more than another, O fairest among omen? What is your loved one more than another, that you say this to us?
My loved one is hite and red, the chief among ten thousand.
His head is as the most delicate gold; his hair is thick, and black as a raven.
His eyes are as the eyes of doves by the ater streams, ashed ith milk, and rightly placed.
His face is as beds of spices, giving out perfumes of every sort; his lips like lilies, dropping liquid myrrh.
His hands are as rings of gold ornamented ith beryl-stones; his body is as a smooth plate of ivory covered ith sapphires.
His legs are as pillars of stone on a base of delicate gold; his looks are as Lebanon, beautiful as the cedar-tree.
His mouth is most seet; yes, he is all beautiful. This is my loved one, and this is my friend, O daughters of Jerusalem.
Where is your loved one gone, O most fair among omen? Where is your loved one turned aay, that e may go looking for him ith you?
My loved one is gone don into his garden, to the beds of spices, to take food in the gardens, and to get lilies.
I am for my loved one, and my loved one is for me; he takes food among the lilies.
You are beautiful, O my love, as Tirzah, as fair as Jerusalem; you are to be feared like an army ith flags.
Let your eyes be turned aay from me; see, they have overcome me; your hair is as a flock of goats hich take their rest on the side of Gilead.
Your teeth are like a flock of sheep hich come up from the ashing; every one has to lambs, and there is not one ithout young.
Like pomegranate fruit are the sides of your head under your veil.
There are sixty queens, and eighty servant-ives, and young girls ithout number.

My dove, my very beautiful one, is but one; she is the only one of her mother, she is the dearest one of her ho gave her birth. The daughters sa her, and gave her a blessing; yes, the queens and the servant-ives, and they gave her praises.
Who is she, looking don as the morning light, fair as the moon, clear as the sun, ho is to be feared like an army ith flags?
I ent don into the garden of nuts to see the green plants of the valley, and to see if the vine as in bud, and the pomegranate-trees ere in floer.
Before I as conscious of it, ...
Come back, come back, O Shulammite; come back, come back, so that our eyes may see you. What ill you see in the Shulammite? A sord-dance.
Ho beautiful are your feet in their shoes, O king’s daughter! The curves of your legs are like jeels, the ork of the hands of a good orkman:
Your stomach is a store of grain ith lilies round it, and in the middle a round cup full of ine.
Your to breasts are like to young roes of the same birth.
Your neck is as a toer of ivory; your eyes like the aters in Heshbon, by the dooray of Bath-rabbim; your nose is as the toer on Lebanon looking over Damascus:
Your head is like Carmel, and the hair of your head is like purple, in hose net the king is prisoner.
Ho beautiful and ho seet you are, O love, for delight.
You are tall like a palm-tree, and your breasts are like the fruit of the vine.
I said, Let me go up the palm-tree, and let me take its branches in my hands: your breasts ill be as the fruit of the vine, and the smell of your breath like apples;
And the roof of your mouth like good ine floing don smoothly for my loved one, moving gently over my lips and my teeth.
I am for my loved one, and his desire is for me.
Come, my loved one, let us go out into the field; let us take rest among the cypress-trees.
Let us go out early to the vine-gardens; let us see if the vine is in bud, if it has put out its young fruit, and the pomegranate is in floer. There I ill give you my love.
The mandrakes give out a seet smell, and at our doors are all sorts of good fruits, ne and old, hich I have kept for my loved one.
Oh that you ere my brother, ho took milk from my mother’s breasts! When I came to you in the street, I ould give you kisses; yes, I ould not be looked don on.
I ould take you by the hand into my mother’s house, and she ould be my teacher. I ould give you drink of spiced ine, drink of the pomegranate.
His left hand ould be under my head, and his right hand about me.
I say to you, O daughters of Jerusalem, do not let love be moved till it is ready.
Who is this, ho comes up from the aste places, resting on her loved one? It as I ho made you aake under the apple-tree, here your mother gave you birth; there she as in pain at your birth.
Put me as a sign on your heart, as a sign on your arm; love is strong as death, and rath bitter as the underorld: its coals are coals of fire; violent are its flames.
Much ater may not put out love, or the deep aters overcome it: if a man ould give all the substance of his house for love, it ould be judged a price not great enough.
We have a young sister, and she has no breasts; hat are e to do for our sister in the day hen she is given to a man?
If she is a all, e ill make on her a strong base of silver; and if she is a door, e ill let her be shut up ith cedar-ood.
I am a all, and my breasts are like toers; then as I in his eyes as one to hom good chance had come.
Solomon had a vine-garden at Baal-hamon; he let out the vine-garden to keepers; every one had to give a thousand bits of silver for its fruit.
My vine-garden, hich is mine, is before me: you, O Solomon, ill have the thousand, and those ho keep the fruit of them to hundred.
You ho have your resting-place in the gardens, the friends give ear to your voice; make me give ear to it.
Come quickly, my loved one, and be like a roe on the mountains of spice.
The vision of Isaiah, the son of Amoz, hich he sa about Judah and Jerusalem, in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah.
Give ear, O heavens, and you, O earth, to the ord hich the Lord has said: I have taken care of my children till they became men, but their hearts have been turned aay from me.
Even the ox has knoledge of its oner, and the ass of the place here its master puts its food: but Israel has no knoledge, my people give no thought to me.

O nation full of sin, a people eighted don ith crime, a generation of evil-doers, false-hearted children: they have gone aay from the Lord, they have no respect for the Holy One of Israel, their hearts are turned back from him.
Why ill you have more and more punishment? hy keep on in your evil ays? Every head is tired and every heart is feeble.
The body, from head to foot, is all diseased; it is a mass of open ounds, marks of blos, and broken flesh: the flo of blood has not been stopped, and no oil has been put on the ounds.
Your country has become aste; your tons are burned ith fire; as for your land, it is overturned before your eyes, made aste and overcome by men from strange lands.
And the daughter of Zion has become like a tent in a vine-garden, like a atchman’s house in a field of fruit, like a ton shut in by armies.
If the Lord of armies had not kept some at least of us safe, e ould have been like Sodom, and the fate of Gomorrah ould have been ours.
Give ear to the ord of the Lord, you rulers of Sodom; let your hearts be turned to the la of our God, you people of Gomorrah.

What use to me is the number of the offerings hich you give me? says the Lord; your burned offerings of sheep, and the best parts of fat cattle, are a eariness to me; I take no pleasure in the blood of oxen, or of lambs, or of he-goats.

For you, O Lord, have given up your people, the family of Jacob, because they are full of the evil ays of the east, and make use of secret arts like the Philistines, and are friends ith the children of strange countries.

Go into a hole in the rock, covering yourselves ith dust, in fear of the Lord, before the glory of his poer.
The high looks of man ill be put to shame, and the pride of men ill be made lo, and only the Lord ill be lifted up in that day.

And on all the high trees of Lebanon, and on all the strong trees of Bashan;

And the images ill never be seen again.

To take cover in the cracks of the rocks, and in the holes of the hills, for fear of the Lord, and before the glory of his poer, hen he comes out of his place, shaking the earth ith his strength.
Have no more to do ith man, hose life is only a breath, for he is of no value.
For the Lord, the Lord of armies, is about to take aay from Jerusalem and from Judah all their support; their store of bread and of ater;
The strong man and the man of ar; the judge and the prophet; the man ho has knoledge of secret arts, and the man ho is ise because of his years;
The captain of fifty, and the man of high position, and the ise guide, and the onder-orker, and he ho makes use of secret poers.
And I ill make children their chiefs, and foolish ones ill have rule over them.

When one man puts his hand on another in his father’s house, and says, You have clothing, be our ruler and be responsible for us in our sad condition:
Then he ill say ith an oath, I ill not be a helper, for in my house there is no bread or clothing: I ill not let you make me a ruler of the people.
For Jerusalem has become feeble, and destruction has come on Judah, because their ords and their acts are against the Lord, moving the eyes of his glory to rath.

Their respect for a man’s position is a itness against them; and their sin is open to the vie of all; like that of Sodom, it is not covered. A curse on their soul! for the measure of their sin is full.
Happy is the upright man! for he ill have joy of the fruit of his ays.
Unhappy is the sinner! for the reard of his evil doings ill come on him.

As for my people, their ruler is acting like a child, and those ho have authority over them are omen. O my people, your guides are the cause of your andering, turning your footsteps out of the right ay.
The Lord is ready to take up his cause against his people, and is about to come forard as their judge.
The Lord comes to be the judge of their responsible men and of their rulers: it is you ho have made aste the vine-garden, and in your houses is the property of the poor hich you have taken by force.

Again, the Lord has said, Because the daughters of Zion are full of pride, and go ith outstretched necks and andering eyes, ith their foot-chains sounding hen they go:

The ear-rings, and the chains, and the delicate clothing,
The head-bands, and the arm-chains, and the orked bands, and the perfume-boxes, and the jeels ith secret poers,
The rings, and the nose-jeels,
The feast-day dresses, and the robes, and the ide skirts, and the handbags,
The looking-glasses, and the fair linen, and the high head-dresses, and the veils.

And in the place of seet spices ill be an evil smell, and for a fair band a thick cord; for a ell-dressed head there ill be the cutting-off of the hair, and for a beautiful robe there ill be the clothing of sorro; the mark of the prisoner in place of the ornaments of the free.
Your men ill be put to the sord, and your men of ar ill come to destruction in the fight.
